danish.title: Syvende bog (1810–11) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: »Sker det nogensinde for dig,« sagde Natasja til sin bror, da de havde sat sig til rette i dagligstuen, »sker det nogensinde for dig, at du føler, som om der ikke er mere at komme — ingenting; at alt det gode er forbi? Og at du ikke ligefrem er ked af det, men trist?«

»Ja selvfølgelig!« svarede han. »Jeg har følt sådan, når alting var i orden, og alle var glade. Den tanke er kommet til mig, at jeg allerede var træt af det hele, og at vi alle må dø. Engang i regimentet var jeg ikke taget med til en fest, hvor der var musik... og pludselig følte jeg mig så nedtrykt...«

»Åh ja, det kender jeg, det kender jeg, det kender jeg!« afbrød Natasja ham. »Da jeg var helt lille, var det også sådan med mig. Kan du huske, da jeg engang blev straffet for noget med blommer? I dansede allesammen, og jeg sad og tudede i skolestuen. Jeg glemmer det aldrig: jeg følte mig trist og ked af det for alle, for mig selv og for alle. Og jeg var uskyldig — det var det, der var det vigtigste,« sagde Natasja. »Kan du huske det?«

»Det husker jeg,« svarede Nikolaj. »Jeg husker, at jeg kom ind til dig bagefter og ville trøste dig, men ved du hvad, jeg skammede mig. Vi var frygteligt fjollede. Jeg havde en sjov dukke dengang og ville give dig den. Kan du huske?«

»Og kan du huske,« spurgte Natasja med et eftertænksomt smil, »da onkel engang for længe, længe siden, da vi var helt små, kaldte os ind i arbejdsværelset — det var i det gamle hus — og det var mørkt — vi gik ind og pludselig stod der...«
»En neger,« faldt Nikolaj ind med et henrykt smil. »Selvfølgelig kan jeg huske det. Selv nu ved jeg ikke, om der virkelig var en neger, eller om vi bare drømte det, eller fik det fortalt.«
»Han var grå, kan du huske, og havde hvide tænder, og stod og kiggede på os...«
»Sonja, kan du huske det?« spurgte Nikolaj.
»Ja, jo, jeg kan også huske noget,« svarede Sonja forsagt.
»Ved du, at jeg har spurgt far og mor om den neger,« sagde Natasja, »og de siger, at der slet ikke var nogen neger. Men I kan jo se, I husker det!«
»Selvfølgelig husker jeg, jeg husker hans tænder, som om jeg lige havde set dem.«
»Hvor er det underligt! Det er som en drøm! Det kan jeg lide.«
»Og kan du huske, da vi trillede hårdkogte æg i balsalen, og pludselig begyndte to gamle koner at snurre rundt på tæppet? Var det virkeligt eller ej? Kan du huske, hvor sjovt det var?«
»Ja, og kan du huske, da far i sin blå frakke affyrede en pistol i indgangen?«

Sådan gennemgik de deres minder, smilende af fornøjelse: ikke alderdommens triste minder, men poetiske, ungdommelige — de indtryk fra ens fjerneste fortid, hvor drømme og virkelighed smelter sammen — og de lo med stille glæde.
Sonja kunne, som altid, ikke helt følge med dem, selvom de delte de samme minder.
Meget af det, de huskede, var gledet ud af hendes hukommelse, og det, hun huskede, vakte ikke den samme poetiske følelse, som de oplevede. Hun nød simpelthen deres glæde og prøvede at passe ind.

Hun deltog kun rigtigt, da de mindedes Sonjas første ankomst. Hun fortalte dem, hvor bange hun havde været for Nikolaj, fordi han havde en snørejakke på, og hendes barnepige havde fortalt hende, at hun også ville blive syet ind med snører.

»Og jeg husker, de fortalte mig, at du var blevet født under en kål,« sagde Natasja, »og jeg husker, at jeg ikke turde lade være med at tro det dengang, men vidste, at det ikke var sandt, og jeg følte mig så utilpas.«
Mens de sad og talte, stak en pige hovedet ind ad den anden dør til dagligstuen.
»De har bragt hanen, frøken,« sagde hun hviskende.
»Den skal ikke bruges, Polja. Sig til dem, at de skal tage den med igen,« svarede Natasja.
Midt i deres samtale i dagligstuen kom Dimmler ind og gik hen til harpen, der stod i et hjørne. Han tog overdækningen af, og harpen gav en skurrende lyd fra sig.
»Hr. Dimmler, vær venlig at spille min yndlingsnokturn af Field,« lød den gamle grevindes stemme fra salonen.
Dimmler slog en akkord an og bemærkede, idet han vendte sig mod Natasja, Nikolaj og Sonja: »Hvor I unge mennesker er stille!«
»Ja, vi filosoferer,« sagde Natasja, idet hun kiggede sig om et øjeblik og så fortsatte samtalen. De drøftede nu drømme.

Dimmler begyndte at spille; Natasja gik på tåspidser lydløst hen til bordet, tog et lys, bar det ud og vendte tilbage og satte sig stille på sin plads igen. Der var mørkt i stuen, især der hvor de sad på sofaen, men gennem de store vinduer faldt det sølvhvide fuldmånelys ind på gulvet. Dimmler var færdig med stykket, men sad stadig og lod fingrene glide blidt over strengene, tydeligvis usikker på, om han skulle stoppe eller spille noget andet.

»Ved I hvad,« sagde Natasja hviskende og rykkede tættere på Nikolaj og Sonja, »at når man bliver ved og ved med at erindre minder, så begynder man til sidst at huske, hvad der skete, før man var til i verden...«
»Det er sjælevandring,« sagde Sonja, der altid havde været flittig med lektierne og huskede alt. »Ægypterne troede, at vores sjæle har levet i dyr og vil vende tilbage til dyr igen.«

»Nej, jeg tror ikke, vi nogensinde har været dyr,« sagde Natasja, stadig hviskende, selvom musikken var ophørt. »Men jeg er sikker på, at vi var engle et eller andet sted deroppe, og at vi har været her, og det er derfor, vi husker...«
»Må jeg slutte mig til jer?« sagde Dimmler, der stille var kommet hen, og han satte sig hos dem.
»Hvis vi har været engle, hvorfor er vi så faldet lavere?« sagde Nikolaj. »Nej, det kan ikke passe!«

»Ikke lavere, hvem sagde vi var lavere?... Hvad ved jeg om, hvad jeg var før?« indvendte Natasja med overbevisning. »Sjælen er udødelig — nå, men så, hvis jeg altid skal leve, må jeg have levet før, levet i en hel evighed.«
»Ja, men det er svært for os at forestille os evigheden,« bemærkede Dimmler, der havde sluttet sig til de unge med et mildt, overbærende smil, men nu talte lige så stille og alvorligt som de.
»Hvorfor er det svært at forestille sig evigheden?« sagde Natasja. »Der er nu i dag, og der vil være i morgen, og altid; og der var i går, og i forgårs...«
»Natasja! Nu er det din tur. Syng noget for mig,« hørte de grevinden sige. »Hvorfor sidder I der som sammensvorne?«
»Mamma, det har jeg slet ikke lyst til,« svarede Natasja, men rejste sig alligevel.

Ingen af dem, ikke engang den midaldrende Dimmler, havde lyst til at afbryde deres samtale og forlade den krog i dagligstuen, men Natasja rejste sig, og Nikolaj satte sig ved klaveret. Stående som sædvanligt midt i salen, og vælgende det sted, hvor klangen var bedst, begyndte Natasja at synge sin mors yndlingssang.

Hun havde sagt, at hun ikke ville synge, men det var længe siden, hun havde sunget, og længe før hun igen sang, som hun gjorde den aften. Greven, der fra sit arbejdsværelse, hvor han talte med Mitenka, hørte hende og som en skoledreng, der har travlt med at komme ud og lege, famlede i sin tale, mens han gav forvalteren ordrer, og til sidst forstummede, mens Mitenka stod foran ham og også lyttede og smilte. Nikolaj vendte ikke blikket fra sin søster og trak vejret i takt med hende. Sonja tænkte, mens hun lyttede, på den uendelige forskel, der var mellem hende selv og hendes veninde, og hvor umuligt det var for hende at være bare tilnærmelsesvis så fortryllende som sin kusine. Den gamle grevinde sad med et lykkeligt, men dog sørgeligt smil og med tårer i øjnene og rystede af og til på hovedet. Hun tænkte på Natasja og på sin egen ungdom, og på hvordan der var noget unaturligt og skræmmende ved dette forestående ægteskab mellem Natasja og fyrst Andrej.
Dimmler, der havde sat sig ved siden af grevinden, lyttede med lukkede øjne.
»Ak, grevinde,« sagde han til sidst, »det er et europæisk talent, hun har intet at lære — hvilken blødhed, ømhed og styrke...«

»Åh, hvor jeg er bange for hende, hvor jeg er bange!« sagde grevinden uden at indse, hvem hun talte til. Hendes moderinstinkt sagde hende, at Natasja havde for meget af noget, og at hun på grund af det ikke ville blive lykkelig. Før Natasja var færdig med at synge, styrtede den fjortenårige Petja henrykt ind for at fortælle, at nogle udklædte var ankommet.
Natasja holdt brat op.
»Idiot!« skreg hun ad sin bror og løb hen til en stol, kastede sig ned i den og hulkede så voldsomt, at hun ikke kunne stoppe i lang tid.
»Det er ingenting, Mamma, det er virkelig ingenting; det var bare Petja, der forskrækkede mig,« sagde hun og prøvede at smile, men tårerne løb stadig, og hulkene kvalte hende stadig.

De udklædte (nogle af husets tyende) udklædt som bjørne, tyrkere, kroværter og damer — skræmmende og morsomme — bragte kulden udefra med sig og en stemning af munterhed, trængte sig først forsigtigt ind i forhallen, og gemte sig bag hinanden, skubbede de sig ind i balsalen, hvor de — i begyndelsen genert, men så mere og mere livligt og hjerteligt — begyndte at synge, danse og lege julelege. Grevinden gik ind i salonen, da hun havde genkendt dem og let ad deres udklædninger. Greven sad i balsalen, smilede strålende og klappede af deltagerne. De unge mennesker var forsvundet.

En halv time senere dukkede der blandt de andre udklædte i balsalen op en gammel dame i krinoline — det var Nikolaj. En tyrkisk pige var Petja. En klovn var Dimmler. En husar var Natasja, og en tsjerkesser var Sonja med brændt kork som overskæg og øjenbryn.
Efter de overbærende overraskelser, mangel på genkendelse og ros fra dem, der ikke selv var udklædte, besluttede de unge, at deres kostumer var så gode, at de burde vises frem andre steder.
Nikolaj, der gerne ville køre en tur med sin trojka, da vejene var i glimrende stand, foreslog at tage en snes af de udklædte tyende med og køre hen til »Onkels«.
»Nej, hvorfor forstyrre den gamle mand?« sagde grevinden. »Desuden er der ikke plads til at vende sig derinde. Hvis I skal af sted, så kør til Meljukoverne.«
Meljukova var en enke, der boede tre verst fra Rostoverne med sin familie og deres huslærere og guvernanter.
»Det er rigtigt, min kære,« sagde den gamle greve, der var helt oplivet. »Jeg klæder mig om med det samme og tager med. Jeg skal nok få Pasjette til at spærre øjnene op.«

Men grevinden ville ikke gå med til, at han tog af sted; han havde haft et dårligt ben de sidste dage. Det blev besluttet, at greven ikke kunne tage med, men at hvis Louisa Ivanovna (Madame Schoss) ville følge med, måtte de unge damer gerne tage til Meljukoverne. Sonja, der ellers var så genert og sky, bad mere indtrængende end nogen anden Louisa Ivanovna om ikke at sige nej.

Sonjas kostume var det bedste af alle. Hendes overskæg og øjenbryn klædte hende usædvanligt godt. Alle sagde, at hun så meget smuk ud, og hun var i et livligt og energisk humør, der var usædvanligt for hende. En indre stemme sagde hende, at nu eller aldrig ville hendes skæbne blive afgjort, og i sit mandlige påklædning virkede hun som en helt anden person. Louisa Ivanovna gav sit samtykke, og i løbet af en halv time kørte fire trojkaslæder med store og små bjælder, med mederne knirkende og fløjtende over den frosne sne, op til indgangspartiet.

Natasja gik forrest med at sætte en munter feriestemning, der bredte sig fra den ene til den anden, voksede og nåede sit højdepunkt, da de alle kom ud i frosten og steg op i slæderne, mens de talte, råbte til hinanden, lo og skreg.

To af trojkaerne var de sædvanlige husslæder, den tredje var den gamle greves med en traver fra Orlov-stutteriet som stangshest, den fjerde var Nikolajs egen med en lille, lodden, sort stangshest. Nikolaj stod i sin gammeldamekjole, hvorover han havde spændt sin husarkappe, midt i slæden med tømmerne i hånden.
Det var så lyst, at han kunne se månelyset genspejlet i seletøjets metalskiver og i hestenes øjne, der så sig uroligt omkring over det støjende selskab under indgangens skygge.
Natasja, Sonja, Madame Schoss og to piger steg op i Nikolajs slæde; Dimmler, hans kone og Petja i den gamle greves, og resten af de udklædte fordelte sig i de to andre slæder.
»Kør forrest, Zakhar!« råbte Nikolaj til sin fars kusk i håb om en chance for at køre ham forbi.

Den gamle greves trojka med Dimmler og hans selskab satte sig i bevægelse, knirkende på sine meder som om den frøs fast til sneen, med sin dybe klokke klingende. Sidehestene pressede mod stangshestens stænger, sank ned i sneen, der var tør og glitrede som sukker, og kastede den op.

Nikolaj satte af sted bag den første slæde; bag ham fulgte de andre med larm og knirkende meder. Først kørte de i roligt trav ad den smalle vej. Mens de kørte forbi haven, faldt de nøgne træers skygger tit tværs over vejen og skjulte det strålende månelys, men så snart de var forbi hegnet, bredte den snedækkede slette badet i månelys sig ud foran dem, glitrende som diamanter og plettet med blålige skygger. Bang, bang! gik den første slæde over et hul i vejens sne, og hver af de andre slæder humpede på samme vis, og idet de groft brød den frostbundne stilhed, begyndte trojkaerne at sætte fart ned ad vejen, den ene efter den anden.
»Et harespor, en masse spor!« lød Natasjas stemme gennem den frostfyldte luft.
»Hvor er det lyst, Nikolaj!« lød Sonjas stemme.

Nikolaj så sig om mod Sonja og bøjede sig ned for at se hendes ansigt tættere på. Et helt nyt, sødt ansigt med sorte øjenbryn og overskæg tittede op mod ham fra hendes sobelskindspels — så nært og dog så fjernt — i månelyset.
»Det plejede at være Sonja,« tænkte han og så nærmere på hende og smilede.
»Hvad er der, Nikolaj?«
»Ingenting,« sagde han og vendte sig igen mod hestene.

Da de nåede ud på den befærdede landevej — poleret af slædemeder og opkørt af grovsko hove, hvis mærker var synlige i månelyset — begyndte hestene af sig selv at trække i tømmerne og sætte farten op. Den nærmeste sidehest, der buede nakken og slog over i kort galop, trak i sine skagler. Stangshesten svajede fra side til side og rørte ørerne som for at spørge: »Er det ikke snart tid til at begynde?« Foran, allerede langt forude, hvor den dybe slædeklokke lød fjernere og fjernere, kunne de sorte heste, som Zakhar kørte, tydeligt ses mod den hvide sne. Fra den slæde hørte man råb, latter og de udklædtes stemmer.
»Hyp, mine kære!« råbte Nikolaj, idet han trak tømmerne til den ene side og svingede pisken.

Det var kun af den skarpere vind, der mødte dem, og af de ryk, sidehestene gav, idet de trak hårdere og stadig øgede deres galop, at man mærkede, hvor hurtigt trojkaen fløj af sted. Nikolaj så sig tilbage. Med skrig, hvin og piskesmæld, der fik selv stangshestene til at galoppere, fulgte de andre slæder. Stangshesten svingede støt under buen over sit hoved uden tanke på at sætte farten ned og klar til at øge den, når det blev forlangt.
Nikolaj overhalede den første slæde. De kørte ned ad en bakke og ud på en bred, opkørt sti hen over en eng nær en flod.

»Hvor er vi?« tænkte han. »Det er vel Kosoj-engen. Men nej — det her er noget nyt, som jeg aldrig har set før. Det er hverken Kosoj-engen eller Djomkin-bakken, og Gud alene ved, hvad det er! Det er noget nyt og fortryllet. Nå, hvad det end er...« Og idet han råbte til sine heste, begyndte han at overhale den første slæde.
Zakhar holdt hestene tilbage og vendte sit ansigt, der allerede var dækket af rimfrost op til øjenbrynene.
Nikolaj gav hestene frie tøjler, og Zakhar strakte armene ud, smældede med tungen og slap sine heste løs.
»Bare pas på, herre!« råbte han.

Hurtigere og hurtigere fløj de to trojkaer side om side, og hurtigere bevægede sig de galopperende sidehestes fødder. Nikolaj begyndte at trække forbi. Zakhar løftede den ene hånd med tømmerne, mens han stadig holdt armene strakte.
»Det tror De ikke, herre!« råbte han.

Nikolaj satte alle sine heste i galop og passerede Zakhar. Hestene overøste dem i slæden med fin, tør sne — ved siden af dem klirrede hurtige klokker, og de fangede forvirrede glimt af hurtigt bevægende ben og skyggen af den trojka, de passerede. Medernes fløjten mod sneen og pigers skrig hørtes fra forskellige sider.
Nikolaj tjekkede atter sine heste og så sig om. De var stadig omgivet af den magiske slette, badet i månelys og oversået med stjerner.

»Zakhar råber, at jeg skal dreje til venstre, men hvorfor til venstre?« tænkte Nikolaj. »Er vi på vej til Meljukoverne? Er det her Meljukovka? Gud alene ved, hvor vi kører hen, og Gud alene ved, hvad der sker med os — men det er meget underligt og behageligt, hvad det end er.« Og han så sig om i slæden.
»Se, hans overskæg og øjenvipper er helt hvide!« sagde en af de fremmede, smukke, ukendte personer — den med de fine øjenbryn og overskæg.
»Jeg tror, at det her plejede at være Natasja,« tænkte Nikolaj, »og det var Madame Schoss, men måske er det ikke, og den tsjerkesser med overskægget kender jeg ikke, men jeg elsker hende.«
»Fryser I?« spurgte han.
De svarede ikke, men begyndte at le. Dimmler råbte noget fra slæden bagved — sikkert noget morsomt — men de kunne ikke høre, hvad han sagde.
»Ja, ja!« svarede nogle stemmer leende.

»Men her var en fortryllet skov med sorte, bevægende skygger, og en glitren af diamanter og en flugt af marmortrapper og sølvtage af fe-bygninger og de skingre skrig af dyr. Og hvis dette virkelig er Meljukovka, så er det endnu mere underligt, at vi kørte Gud ved hvorhen og er endt i Meljukovka,« tænkte Nikolaj.
Det var virkelig Meljukovka, og piger og tjenere med glade ansigter kom løbende ud på trappen med stearinlys.
»Hvem er det?« spurgte nogen på trappen.
»De udklædte fra greven. Jeg kan se det på hestene,« svarede nogle stemmer.

english.title: Book Seven (1810 - 11) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: "Does it ever happen to you," said Natasha to her brother when they had settled down in the sitting room, "does it ever happen that you feel as if nothing more is going to come — nothing — that everything good is already past? And not exactly bored, but sad?"

"Absolutely!" he said. "I've felt that way when everything was perfectly fine and everyone was cheerful. The thought would come to me that I was already tired of it all, and that we must all die. Once in the regiment I didn't go to some party where there was music... and suddenly I felt so low..."

"Oh yes, I know, I know, I know!" Natasha interrupted. "When I was little it used to happen to me. Remember when I was punished about those plums? You were all dancing, and I sat sobbing in the schoolroom? I'll never forget it — I felt sad and sorry for everyone, for myself and for everyone. And I was innocent — that was the main thing," said Natasha. "Do you remember?"

"I remember," answered Nicholas. "I remember coming to you afterward, wanting to comfort you — but, you know, I felt ashamed. We were terribly silly. I had a funny doll then and wanted to give it to you. Do you remember?"

"And do you remember," Natasha asked with a pensive smile, "how once, long, long ago, when we were quite small, Uncle called us into the study — that was in the old house — and it was dark — we went in and suddenly there stood..."
"A Black man," chimed in Nicholas with a smile of delight. "Of course I remember. Even now I don't know whether there really was a Black man, or if we only dreamed it or were told about it."
"He was gray, remember, and had white teeth, and he stood there looking at us..."
"Sonya, do you remember?" asked Nicholas.
"Yes, yes — I remember something too," Sonya answered timidly.
"You know, I've asked Papa and Mama about that man," said Natasha, "and they say there was no one at all. But you see — you remember!"
"Of course I do — I remember his teeth as if I'd just seen them."
"How strange it is! It's like a dream. I love that."
"And do you remember how we rolled hard-boiled eggs in the ballroom, and suddenly two old women started spinning around on the carpet? Was that real or not? Do you remember how funny it was?"
"Yes, and remember how Papa in his blue overcoat fired a gun on the porch?"

So they went through their memories, smiling with pleasure — not the sad memories of old age, but poetic, youthful ones, those impressions from one's most distant past where dreams and reality blend — and they laughed with quiet contentment.
Sonya, as always, couldn't quite keep pace with them, though they shared the same memories.
Much of what they remembered had slipped from her mind, and what she did recall didn't stir the same poetic feeling they experienced. She simply enjoyed their pleasure and tried to share in it.

She only truly participated when they recalled Sonya's first arrival. She told them how afraid she had been of Nicholas because he was wearing a braided jacket and her nurse had told her she too would be sewn up with braids.
"And I remember them saying you had been born under a cabbage," said Natasha. "I remember that I didn't dare not believe it, but I knew it wasn't true, and I felt so uncomfortable."
While they were talking, a maid poked her head in through the other door of the sitting room.
"They've brought the rooster, miss," she said in a whisper.
"It's not needed, Polya. Tell them to take it away," replied Natasha.
In the middle of their conversation, Dimmler came in and walked over to the harp standing in the corner. He removed its cloth covering, and the harp gave out a jarring sound.
"Mr. Dimmler, please play my favorite nocturne by Field," came the old countess's voice from the drawing room.
Dimmler struck a chord and, turning to Natasha, Nicholas, and Sonya, remarked: "How quiet you young people are!"
"Yes, we're philosophizing," said Natasha, glancing up for a moment, then continuing the conversation. They were now discussing dreams.

Dimmler began to play; Natasha tiptoed to the table, took a candle, carried it out, and returned, seating herself quietly in her former place. It was dark in the room, especially where they sat on the sofa, but through the large windows the silvery light of the full moon fell on the floor. Dimmler finished the piece but remained at the harp, softly running his fingers over the strings, clearly undecided whether to stop or play something else.

"Do you know," said Natasha in a whisper, moving closer to Nicholas and Sonya, "that when you keep going back and back through your memories, you finally start to remember things that happened before you were even born..."
"That's metempsychosis," said Sonya, who had always been a good student and remembered everything. "The Egyptians believed that our souls once lived in animals and will return to animals again."

"No, I don't believe we were ever in animals," said Natasha, still whispering even though the music had stopped. "But I'm certain we were angels somewhere up there, and we've been here before, and that's why we remember..."
"May I join you?" said Dimmler, who had come up quietly, and he sat down with them.
"If we were angels, why have we fallen lower?" said Nicholas. "No, that can't be!"

"Not lower — who said we were lower?... How do I know what I was before?" Natasha shot back with conviction. "The soul is immortal — well then, if I shall always live, I must have lived before, lived for a whole eternity."
"Yes, but it's hard for us to imagine eternity," remarked Dimmler, who had joined the young people with a mildly patronizing smile but now spoke as quietly and seriously as they did.
"Why is it hard to imagine eternity?" said Natasha. "It's today now, and it will be tomorrow, and always; and there was yesterday, and the day before..."
"Natasha! Your turn now. Sing something for me," called the countess. "Why are you sitting there like conspirators?"
"Mama, I really don't want to," replied Natasha, but she got up all the same.

None of them — not even the middle-aged Dimmler — wanted to break off their conversation and leave that corner of the sitting room. But Natasha stood up, and Nicholas sat down at the clavichord. Standing as she always did in the middle of the hall, choosing the spot with the best acoustics, Natasha began to sing her mother's favorite song.

She had said she didn't want to sing, but it had been a long time since she had sung, and a long time before she would sing again as she did that evening. The count, from his study where he was talking with Mitenka, heard her — and like a schoolboy rushing out to play, he stumbled over his words while giving orders to the steward and finally stopped, while Mitenka stood before him also listening and smiling. Nicholas didn't take his eyes off his sister and drew breath in time with her. Sonya, listening, thought of the vast difference between herself and her friend and how impossible it was for her to be anything like as captivating as her cousin. The old countess sat with a blissful yet sad smile and tears in her eyes, shaking her head now and then. She was thinking about Natasha and about her own youth, and about how there was something unnatural and frightening in this approaching marriage of Natasha and Prince Andrew.
Dimmler, who had seated himself beside the countess, listened with closed eyes.
"Ah, Countess," he said at last, "that is a European talent — she has nothing to learn. What softness, tenderness, and strength..."

"Ah, how afraid I am for her, how afraid!" said the countess, not realizing whom she was speaking to. Her maternal instinct told her that there was too much of something in Natasha and that because of this she would not be happy. Before Natasha had finished singing, fourteen-year-old Petya burst in excitedly to announce that mummers had arrived.
Natasha stopped abruptly.
"Idiot!" she screamed at her brother and, running to a chair, threw herself into it, sobbing so violently that she couldn't stop for a long time.
"It's nothing, Mama, really nothing — Petya just startled me," she said, trying to smile, but tears kept flowing and sobs still shook her.

The mummers — house serfs dressed up as bears, Turks, innkeepers, and fine ladies — frightening and funny, bringing with them the cold from outside and a feeling of gaiety, crowded at first timidly into the anteroom, then, hiding behind one another, pushed into the ballroom where, shyly at first and then more and more merrily and wholeheartedly, they began singing, dancing, and playing Christmas games. The countess, after identifying them and laughing at their costumes, went into the drawing room. The count sat in the ballroom, beaming and applauding. The young people had vanished.

Half an hour later there appeared among the other mummers: an old lady in a hooped skirt — Nicholas; a Turkish girl — Petya; a clown — Dimmler; a hussar — Natasha; and a Circassian — Sonya, with mustache and eyebrows drawn in burnt cork.

After the condescending surprise, the failure to recognize anyone, and the praise from the people who were not in costume, the young people decided that their outfits were so good they needed to be shown elsewhere.
Nicholas, who was eager to take them all for a ride in his troika since the roads were in splendid condition, proposed to bring about a dozen of the serf mummers and drive to "Uncle's."
"No, why bother the old fellow?" said the countess. "Besides, you wouldn't have room to turn around there. If you must go, go to the Melyukovs'."
Melyukova was a widow who lived with her family and their tutors and governesses three miles from the Rostovs.
"That's right, my dear," chimed in the old count, thoroughly enthused. "I'll dress up right away and go with them. I'll make Pashette's eyes pop."

But the countess wouldn't agree to his going; he'd had a bad leg for days. It was decided that the count must stay, but that if Louisa Ivanovna — Madame Schoss — would go with them, the young ladies could go to the Melyukovs'. Sonya, usually so timid and shy, begged Louisa Ivanovna more urgently than anyone not to refuse.

Sonya's costume was the best of all. Her mustache and eyebrows were extraordinarily becoming. Everyone said she looked very handsome, and she was in a spirited, energetic mood quite unlike her usual self. Some inner voice told her that tonight or never her fate would be decided, and in her male attire she seemed a completely different person. Louisa Ivanovna agreed to come, and within half an hour four troikas with large and small bells, their runners squeaking and whistling over the frozen snow, pulled up to the porch.

Natasha was the first to set the merry holiday mood, and this merriment, passing from one person to the next, grew stronger until it reached its peak when they all came out into the frost and got into the sleighs, talking, calling to one another, laughing, and shouting.

Two of the troikas were ordinary household sleighs; the third was the old count's, drawn by a trotter from the Orlov stud; the fourth was Nicholas's own, with a shaggy little black shaft horse. Nicholas, in his old-lady costume belted with a hussar overcoat, stood in the middle of his sleigh, reins in hand.

It was so light that he could see the moonlight reflected off the metal harness disks and off the eyes of the horses, who looked around nervously at the noisy party gathered under the shadow of the porch roof.
Natasha, Sonya, Madame Schoss, and two maids got into Nicholas's sleigh; Dimmler, his wife, and Petya into the old count's; and the rest of the mummers took the other two sleighs.
"You go first, Zakhar!" Nicholas shouted to his father's coachman, hoping for a chance to race past him.

The old count's troika, carrying Dimmler and his party, started forward with a squeak of runners as if freezing to the snow, its deep-toned bell clanging. The side horses, pressing against the shafts, sank into the dry, diamond-glinting snow and tossed it up.

Nicholas set off behind the first sleigh; behind him the others followed noisily, their runners squeaking. At first they drove at a steady trot along the narrow road. While they passed the garden the shadows of bare trees fell across the road, hiding the brilliant moonlight, but as soon as they were past the fence the snowy plain — bathed in moonlight and motionless — stretched out before them, glittering like diamonds and mottled with bluish shadows. Bang, bang! went the first sleigh over a rut in the frozen road, and each sleigh behind it jolted the same way, and rudely breaking the frost-bound stillness, the troikas began to fly along one after another.
"A hare's track — lots of tracks!" rang out Natasha's voice through the frost-bound air.
"How bright it is, Nicholas!" came Sonya's voice.

Nicholas glanced around at Sonya and bent down to see her face more closely. A quite new, sweet face with black eyebrows and a mustache peeked up at him from her sable fur — so close and yet so far away in the moonlight.
"That used to be Sonya," thought he, and looked at her more closely and smiled.
"What is it, Nicholas?"
"Nothing," he said, and turned back to the horses.

When they reached the beaten highway — polished by sleigh runners and rutted by rough-shod hooves, the marks of which shone in the moonlight — the horses began pulling at the reins of their own accord and picked up speed. The near horse arched its head, broke into a short canter, and tugged at its traces. The shaft horse swayed from side to side, flicking its ears as if asking: "Isn't it time to begin?" Ahead, already far in front, the deep bell of the lead sleigh rang out more and more distantly, and the black horses driven by Zakhar were clearly visible against the white snow. From that sleigh came shouts, laughter, and the mummers' voices.
"Gee up, my darlings!" shouted Nicholas, pulling the reins to one side and cracking the whip.

Only the sharper wind meeting them and the jerking of the side horses — pulling ever harder and quickening their gallop — showed how fast the troika was flying. Nicholas looked back. With screams, squeals, and cracking whips that sent even the shaft horses into a gallop, the other sleighs followed. The shaft horse swung steadily under the arch over its head, never thinking of slowing down, ready to put on more speed when asked.
Nicholas overtook the first sleigh. They were racing downhill and out across a broad, well-trodden track through a meadow near the river.

"Where are we?" he thought. "It must be the Kosoy meadow. But no — this is something I've never seen before. This isn't the Kosoy meadow or the Demkin hill, and heaven only knows what it is! It's something new and enchanted. Well, whatever it may be..." And shouting to his horses, he began to pass the first sleigh.
Zakhar held back his horses and turned his face — already covered with frost up to his eyebrows — toward them.
Nicholas gave his horses their head, and Zakhar, stretching out his arms, clicked his tongue and let his horses go.
"Now watch yourself, master!" he cried.

Faster and faster the two troikas flew side by side, and faster moved the galloping legs of the side horses. Nicholas began to pull ahead. Zakhar, keeping his arms stretched out, raised one hand with the reins.
"Not a chance, master!" he shouted.

Nicholas pushed all his horses into a gallop and flew past Zakhar. The horses sprayed the fine, dry snow into the faces of those in the sleigh — beside them sounded the quick jingling of bells, and they caught confused glimpses of swiftly moving legs and the shadow of the troika they were overtaking. The whistling of runners on snow and the shrieks of girls could be heard from different sides.
Checking his horses again, Nicholas looked around. They were still surrounded by the magic plain bathed in moonlight and spangled with stars.

"Zakhar is shouting that I should turn left — but why left?" thought Nicholas. "Are we getting to the Melyukovs'? Is this Melyukovka? Heaven only knows where we're going, and heaven knows what's happening to us — but it's very strange and wonderful, whatever it is." And he looked around in the sleigh.
"Look — his mustache and eyelashes are all white!" said one of the strange, pretty, unfamiliar people — the one with the fine eyebrows and mustache.
"I think this used to be Natasha," thought Nicholas, "and that was Madame Schoss — but maybe not. And this Circassian with the mustache I don't know, but I love her."
"Aren't you cold?" he asked.
They didn't answer but started laughing. Dimmler shouted something from the sleigh behind — probably something funny — but they couldn't make out what he said.
"Yes, yes!" some voices answered, laughing.

"But here was a fairy forest with black moving shadows and a glitter of diamonds and a flight of marble steps and the silver roofs of fairy buildings and the shrill cries of strange creatures. And if this really is Melyukovka, it is stranger still that we drove heaven knows where and have arrived at Melyukovka," thought Nicholas.
It really was Melyukovka, and maids and footmen with merry faces came running out onto the porch carrying candles.
"Who is it?" asked someone from the porch.
"The mummers from the count's. I know by the horses," replied several voices.
